standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 5 (the likelihood function as a random function), with the domain and codomain corrected
canonical_claim.location: p. 186 (PDF p. 204), footnote 5, attached to the sentence after Definition 5.2.1
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed footnote] Formally, we would say that the likelihood function is itself a random function, $\mathcal{L} : \Omega \to \mathscr{L}$, where $\mathscr{L}$ is the space of functions $L : \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]$. [Corrected footnote] Formally, we would say that the likelihood function is itself a random function, $\mathcal{L} : \Omega \to \mathscr{L}$, where, for finite-valued likelihoods, $\mathscr{L}$ is the space of functions $L : \boldsymbol\Theta \to [0, \infty)$. [Formal content] For a parametric model $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$ with $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$ and each $g(\cdot, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ a finite-valued conditional PMF or PDF: for every $\omega \in \Omega$, the map $\mathbf{t} \mapsto \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y(\omega), \mathbf{X}(\omega)) = g(Y(\omega), \mathbf{X}(\omega); \mathbf{t})$ is a function from $\boldsymbol\Theta$ to $[0, \infty)$. Its domain is $\boldsymbol\Theta$, which is a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ only when $\tau = 1$; and its values need not lie in $[0, 1]$ when $g$ is a PDF: in the classical linear model, $\phi(y; (\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2))$ at $y = \mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta$ equals $\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$, which exceeds 1 whenever $\sigma < \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] Parametric Model. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): the footnote types the likelihood as a function from $\mathbb{R}$ to $[0, 1]$, which is right only for a scalar parameter and a discrete outcome; the body definition is correct and nothing uses the footnote. The normal-density instance is an illustration added here of the validator's statement that 'a density likelihood can exceed one'.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 10 (Example 5.2.4), corrected: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^2$ is the ML estimator of $\sigma^2$, not of $\sigma$
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed footnote] We do not need to estimate $\sigma$ here, but simple algebraic manipulations show that its ML estimator will equal $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^2$, or the plug-in sample variance of the residuals.) [Corrected footnote] We do not need to estimate $\sigma^2$ here, but simple algebraic manipulations show that its ML estimator will equal $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^2$, or the plug-in sample variance of the residuals. [Formal content] In the setting of Example 5.2.4, let $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ minimize $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{b})^2$ over $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}$ and let $Q = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^2$. If $Q > 0$, then the log-likelihood $\log\mathcal{L}((\mathbf{b}, s)|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = -n\log s - \frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{1}{2s^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{b})^2$ is maximized over $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}$ and $s > 0$ at $\mathbf{b} = \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and $s = \hat\sigma_{ML} = \sqrt{Q/n}$; so the ML estimator of $\sigma^2$ is $Q/n$ and the ML estimator of $\sigma$ is $\sqrt{Q/n}$. Because the residuals have mean zero when the regression includes an intercept (Theorem 4.1.5), $Q/n$ is the plug-in sample variance of the residuals (Definition 3.2.18).

For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood. [Example 5.2.4, p. 190 (PDF p. 208)] $Y = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ conditional on $\mathbf{X}$; $\mathcal{L}((\mathbf{b}, s)|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{s\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{\frac{-(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{b})^2}{2s^2}}$. [Definition 3.2.18, p. 106 (PDF p. 124)] the plug-in sample variance is $\overline{X^2} - \overline{X}^2$. [Theorem 4.1.5, p. 149 (PDF p. 167)] $\overline{e} = 0$ for the OLS residuals.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): $\sigma$ denotes the standard deviation in the example, but the footnote gives the residual sum of squares over $n$ as its estimate; the footnote's own gloss says 'sample variance'. (It also has an unmatched closing parenthesis.) The condition $Q > 0$ is needed for the maximum over $s$ to be attained; the validator notes that no existence claim is established for exact-fit samples. The maximization in $s$: $\frac{d}{ds}\left(-n\log s - \frac{Q}{2s^2}\right) = -\frac{n}{s} + \frac{Q}{s^3}$, positive for $s^2 < Q/n$ and negative for $s^2 > Q/n$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 5.2.10 (Maximum Likelihood Plug-In Estimator), the indicator in both displays of $\hat F_{ML}$, with its subscripts corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Definition 5.2.10. Maximum Likelihood Plug-In Estimator. For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ with common CDF $F$, the ML plug-in estimator of $\psi = T(F)$ is $\hat\psi_{ML} = T(\hat F_{ML})$, where $\hat F_{ML}(y, \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{I}\left(X_{[1]i} \le x_{[1]i}, X_{[2]} \le x_{[2]i}, ..., X_{[K]i} \le x_{[x]}\right)\sum_{v \le y} g(v, \mathbf{X}_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})\right)$ if $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$ is a PMF, and $\hat F_{ML}(y, \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{I}\left(X_{[1]i} \le x_{[1]i}, X_{[2]} \le x_{[2]i}, ..., X_{[K]i} \le x_{[x]}\right)\int_{-\infty}^{y} g(v, \mathbf{X}_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})dv\right)$ if $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$ is a PDF. [Corrected displays] $\hat F_{ML}(y, \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{I}\left(X_{[1]i} \le x_{[1]}, X_{[2]i} \le x_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]i} \le x_{[K]}\right)\sum_{v \le y} g(v, \mathbf{X}_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})\right)$ if $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$ is a PMF, and $\hat F_{ML}(y, \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{I}\left(X_{[1]i} \le x_{[1]}, X_{[2]i} \le x_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]i} \le x_{[K]}\right)\int_{-\infty}^{y} g(v, \mathbf{X}_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})dv\right)$ if $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$ is a PDF. [Statement attached to the definition, p. 198] The definition follows from invoking the Law of Iterated Expectations and substituting sample quantities for population analogs. [Formal content] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X} = (X_{[1]}, ..., X_{[K]})$ with joint CDF $F$ and conditional PDF $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}$: $F(y, \mathbf{x}) = \Pr[Y \le y, X_{[1]} \le x_{[1]}, ..., X_{[K]} \le x_{[K]}] = \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{I}(X_{[1]} \le x_{[1]}, ..., X_{[K]} \le x_{[K]})\int_{-\infty}^{y} f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(v|\mathbf{X})dv\right]$ (with a sum over $v \le y$ in the PMF case). The corrected $\hat F_{ML}$ replaces the expectation by the sample mean over $i$ and $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(v|\mathbf{X}_i)$ by $g(v, \mathbf{X}_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})$; if each $g(\cdot, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})$ is a PMF or PDF, $\hat F_{ML}$ is a joint CDF on $\mathbb{R}^{K+1}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] a statistical functional $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$ on the set of all possible CDFs; [footnote 27, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] the definitions generalize to the multivariate case, with the joint empirical CDF $\hat F(x, y) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x, Y \le y)}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): in both displays the indicator prints the thresholds as $x_{[1]i}$ and $x_{[2]i}$ (with an observation index), omits the index $i$ on $X_{[2]}$, and prints $x_{[x]}$ for $x_{[K]}$; the literal expression is not defined in the book's notation, and the intended indicator follows from the construction described beneath it. This is a correction to a definition; the provable content is the population identity that motivates it. Part of headline claim P001-ch05-H6.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Example 6.1.2 (Bounding the Expected Value), the upper-bound instruction, corrected ('highest' for 'lowest'); with Theorem 6.1.3 (Sharp Bounds for the Expected Value)
canonical_claim.location: Example 6.1.2: pp. 209–210 (PDF pp. 227–228). Theorem 6.1.3: p. 210 (PDF p. 228), proof on p. 211 (PDF p. 229). Section 6.1.1, first paragraphs: p. 209
canonical_claim.statement: [Rule, p. 209, as printed] Suppose that $Y_i$ is bounded: $\mathrm{Supp}[Y_i] \subseteq [a, b]$, for some $a \le b$. ... To compute a lower bound, assume that all missing values of $Y_i$ equal the lowest possible value, $a$. For an upper bound, assume that all missing values of $Y_i$ equal the highest possible value, $b$. [Example 6.1.2, pp. 209–210] Suppose that $Y_i$ is binary: $\mathrm{Supp}[Y_i] \subseteq \{0, 1\} \subseteq [0, 1]$. We might observe the following data: units $1, ..., 6$ with $Y_i^* = 1, -99, 1, 0, 1, -99$ and $R_i = 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0$. For units 2 and 6, we only know that $Y_i \in \{0, 1\}$. To estimate a lower bound, we replace these missing values with the lowest possible value: $Y_i = 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0$. Then, using the sample mean as a plug-in estimator for the expected value, our estimated lower bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is $\frac{1}{2}$. [Printed] Likewise, to estimate an upper bound, we replace these missing values with the lowest possible values: $Y_i = 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1$. Thus, our estimated upper bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is $\frac{5}{6}$. [Corrected sentence] Likewise, to estimate an upper bound, we replace these missing values with the highest possible values: $Y_i = 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1$. Thus, our estimated upper bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is $\frac{5}{6}$. [Formal content of the example] With $a = 0$, $b = 1$ and the six observations above: $\frac{1}{6}\sum_{i=1}^{6}(Y_i^*R_i + a(1 - R_i)) = \frac{1 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 0}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{6}\sum_{i=1}^{6}(Y_i^*R_i + b(1 - R_i)) = \frac{1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$; imputing the lowest value 0 in the upper-bound table would give $\frac{1}{2}$ again, not $\frac{5}{6}$. [Theorem 6.1.3, p. 210, as printed; unchanged] Sharp Bounds for the Expected Value. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[Y_i] \subseteq [a, b]$ and $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$. Then $\mathrm{E}[Y_i] \in \left[\mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1]\Pr[R_i = 1] + a\Pr[R_i = 0],\ \mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1]\Pr[R_i = 1] + b\Pr[R_i = 0]\right]$. [Sharpness, as asserted in the prose on pp. 209 and 212: 'bounds that cannot be improved upon without further assumptions'; 'even with full knowledge of the joint distribution of $(Y_i^*, R_i)$, we can do no better than the above bounds'] For every value $c$ in the interval of Theorem 6.1.3 there are random variables $(Y_i', R_i')$ with $\mathrm{Supp}[Y_i'] \subseteq [a, b]$ whose observable pair $(Y_i'^*, R_i')$ has the same joint distribution as $(Y_i^*, R_i)$ and for which $\mathrm{E}[Y_i'] = c$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the stable outcomes model $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ with response indicator $R_i$ (Definition 6.1.1); i.i.d. sampling of units; MCAR (Definition 6.1.5); MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 6.1.8) and conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); the response propensity function $p_R$ (Definition 6.1.11); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] Stable Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): 'lowest' is printed for 'highest' in the sentence introducing the upper-bound table; the table (missing values filled with 1) and the bound $\frac{5}{6}$ are right. The target also carries the identification part of headline claim P001-ch06-H1 (the bounds of Theorem 6.1.3 and their sharpness), which held up. The theorem as boxed states only that $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ lies in the interval; sharpness is stated in prose and is given here as the existence statement it amounts to (when $\Pr[R_i = 0] > 0$ the missing outcomes can be given any conditional mean in $[a, b]$). $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$ is implied by $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, so $\mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1]$ is defined. The estimation part (Theorem 6.1.4) is a separate target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The paragraph after Example 6.2.5 (Imputation with the Propensity Score): the comparison of donors for unit 2, corrected ($p_R(\mathbf{X}_2)$ for $p_R(\mathbf{X}_1)$); with the hot deck estimate of the example
canonical_claim.location: Example 6.2.5: pp. 224–225 (PDF pp. 242–243). Paragraph after it: p. 225 (PDF p. 243)
canonical_claim.statement: [Example 6.2.5, as printed] Suppose that we had the following data: units $1, ..., 6$ with $Y_i = 2, ?, 3, 10, 12, ?$; $R_i = 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0$; $X_{[1]i} = 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1$; $X_{[2]i} = 3, 7, 9, 5, 4, 3$; $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) = 0.33, 0.14, 0.73, 0.35, 0.78, 0.70$. ... Hot deck imputation is perhaps one of the simplest imputation estimators: for each missing unit, find the observed unit that is closest on $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ and use that unit's outcome to fill in the missing outcome. In this example, we have two unobserved outcomes to impute. Unit 2 has the propensity score $p_R(\mathbf{X}_2) = 0.14$. The observed unit with the closest propensity score is unit 1 with $p_R(\mathbf{X}_1) = 0.33$, so we use $Y_1 = 2$ to impute $Y_2$. Likewise, unit 6 has the propensity score $p_R(\mathbf{X}_6) = 0.70$, and the observed units with closest propensity score is unit 3 with $p_R(\mathbf{X}_3) = 0.73$, so we use $Y_3 = 3$ to impute $Y_6$. This yields [the completed outcomes $2, 2, 3, 10, 12, 3$]. So the hot deck imputation estimate of $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is $\frac{32}{6} = \frac{16}{3} \approx 5.33$. [Printed sentence, p. 225] In the above example, we used $Y_1 = 2$ to impute $Y_2$ because $p_R(\mathbf{X}_1) = 0.33$ is closest to $p_R(\mathbf{X}_2) = 0.14$. But $p_R(\mathbf{X}_4) = 0.35$ is almost as close to $p_R(\mathbf{X}_1)$, so $Y_4 = 10$ probably also gives us some information about $\mathrm{E}[Y_i|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) = 0.14]$. [Corrected sentence] ... But $p_R(\mathbf{X}_4) = 0.35$ is almost as close to $p_R(\mathbf{X}_2)$, so $Y_4 = 10$ probably also gives us some information about $\mathrm{E}[Y_i|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) = 0.14]$. [Formal content] With the propensity scores of the table: among the observed units $\{1, 3, 4, 5\}$, the distances to $p_R(\mathbf{X}_2) = 0.14$ are $|0.33 - 0.14| = 0.19$, $|0.73 - 0.14| = 0.59$, $|0.35 - 0.14| = 0.21$, $|0.78 - 0.14| = 0.64$, so the nearest observed unit is unit 1 and the second nearest is unit 4, at a distance larger by $0.02$; the distances to $p_R(\mathbf{X}_6) = 0.70$ are $0.37, 0.03, 0.35, 0.08$, so the nearest observed unit is unit 3. The completed outcomes are $(2, 2, 3, 10, 12, 3)$ and their mean is $\frac{32}{6} = \frac{16}{3}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the stable outcomes model (Definition 6.1.1), MAR (Definition 6.1.8), the response propensity function $p_R$ (Definition 6.1.11). [Section 6.2.3, p. 224 (PDF p. 242)] hot deck imputation, using nearest-neighbor matching with the propensity score (which, for the moment, we assume is known). Footnote 13 (p. 225) explains the name.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): a wrong subscript in an illustrative sentence; the relevant comparison is between the distances of units 1 and 4 from unit 2 (0.19 and 0.21), whereas the printed sentence compares unit 4 with unit 1 (distance 0.02). No donor, imputed value or estimate changes. The same finding lists six slips in running prose (pp. 208, 216, 219, 225, 226, 234) that have no mathematical content; 'the observed units with closest propensity score is unit 3' is as printed. The target records the corrected comparison as exact arithmetic on the example's table and checks the example's estimate; it is part of headline claim P001-ch06-H5 (hot deck matching on the propensity score).
